question: To what category of real property does RPL Section 443's agency disclosure requirement apply?
choice_a: Residential real property only -- property used or occupied (or intended to be) as a home or residence, improved by a one-to-four family dwelling or a condominium/cooperative apartment
choice_b: All real property of any kind, including undeveloped commercial and industrial land
choice_c: Only rental apartment buildings with five or more units
choice_d: Only property being sold at a price above the local median sale price
explanation: RPL Section 443's definitions limit its scope to residential real property -- property used or occupied, or intended to be used or occupied, as a home or residence, improved by a one-to-four family dwelling or condominium/cooperative apartments.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(1) -- definition of 'residential real property'

question: Does RPL Section 443's statutory definition of 'residential real property' include unimproved (vacant) land?
choice_a: No -- the definition specifically excludes unimproved real property, even if it is ultimately intended for residential use
choice_b: Yes -- any vacant parcel zoned residential is automatically covered
choice_c: Yes -- vacant land is covered as long as a survey has been completed
choice_d: Yes -- vacant land is covered only in counties outside New York City
explanation: The statute's definition of residential real property expressly carves out unimproved real property, so a vacant land parcel falls outside RPL Section 443's disclosure requirement regardless of its eventual intended use.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(1) -- 'residential real property' excludes unimproved land

question: A licensee is listing a large commercial office building for sale. Is the DOS-1736 agency disclosure form legally required under RPL Section 443 for this listing?
choice_a: No -- RPL Section 443 by its terms applies only to residential real property, so this purely commercial listing falls outside the statute's scope
choice_b: Yes -- the statute applies identically to commercial and residential property
choice_c: Yes, but only if the building contains a superintendent's residential unit
choice_d: No -- commercial listings are exempt only if the buyer is also a licensed broker
explanation: Because RPL Section 443 defines its scope as limited to residential real property, a transaction involving a purely commercial office building is not subject to the statute's mandatory disclosure requirement.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(1)-(2) -- scope limited to residential real property

question: A broker takes a listing for an unimproved, undeveloped parcel of raw land with no structures on it. Under RPL Section 443's own definitions, is this listing within the statute's scope?
choice_a: No -- the statutory definition of residential real property excludes unimproved land, so this listing falls outside RPL Section 443's mandatory disclosure requirement
choice_b: Yes -- all vacant land automatically qualifies as residential real property
choice_c: Yes, but only if the listing broker is also acting as the buyer's agent
choice_d: No -- but only because the parcel is larger than five acres
explanation: Since RPL Section 443 defines residential real property to exclude unimproved land, a raw, undeveloped parcel does not trigger the statute's disclosure requirement even though it might eventually be developed for residential use.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(1) -- unimproved land excluded from scope

question: Under RPL Section 443, when must a listing agent provide the agency disclosure form to a prospective seller or landlord?
choice_a: Prior to entering into the listing agreement with the seller/landlord -- a distinct trigger point from the 'first substantive contact' standard that applies when a seller's agent deals with a buyer
choice_b: At the closing table, alongside the deed
choice_c: Only if the seller specifically asks for a copy of the form
choice_d: Within 30 days after the listing agreement is signed
explanation: RPL Section 443 requires a listing agent to provide the disclosure form to the seller/landlord before entering into the listing agreement itself -- a trigger tied to that specific agreement, distinct from the 'first substantive contact' standard used when the same agent later deals with a buyer.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(3)(a) -- listing agent disclosure trigger

question: A buyer's agent represents a buyer under RPL Section 443. What two distinct triggers govern when that agent must provide the agency disclosure form?
choice_a: Prior to entering into the buyer agency agreement with the buyer, and at the time of first substantive contact with the seller or the seller's agent
choice_b: Only once, at the closing table, regardless of which party is involved
choice_c: Only when the buyer asks the agent to represent them in writing, with no obligation toward the seller's side at all
choice_d: Only at first substantive contact with the buyer, with no separate obligation toward the seller or seller's agent
explanation: A buyer's agent has two distinct disclosure triggers under RPL Section 443: providing the form to the buyer before entering into a buyer agency agreement, and providing the form to the seller or seller's agent at first substantive contact.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(3)(c) -- buyer's agent dual disclosure triggers

question: A buyer signs a written buyer agency agreement with an agent. The agent presents the RPL Section 443 disclosure form to the buyer for the first time only after the agreement is already signed. Is this compliant?
choice_a: No -- the disclosure form must be provided to the buyer prior to entering into the buyer agency agreement, not afterward
choice_b: Yes -- as long as the form is presented before the first offer is submitted
choice_c: Yes -- the statute imposes no particular sequencing between the agreement and the disclosure form
choice_d: Yes -- because the buyer, not the agent, controls when disclosure occurs
explanation: RPL Section 443 requires a buyer's agent to provide the disclosure form prior to entering into the buyer agency agreement, so presenting the form only after the agreement is signed reverses the required sequence and is noncompliant.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(3)(c) -- disclosure must precede buyer agency agreement

question: How long must a licensee retain a copy of a signed RPL Section 443 disclosure acknowledgment?
choice_a: Not less than three years
choice_b: There is no minimum retention period specified in the statute
choice_c: Not less than ten years
choice_d: Only until the transaction closes, after which the record may be destroyed
explanation: RPL Section 443 requires the agent to maintain a copy of the signed acknowledgment for not less than three years, giving DOS and the parties a documented compliance trail well beyond the closing date.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(3) -- three-year retention of signed acknowledgment

question: Besides retaining an internal office copy, what else must a licensee do with the signed RPL Section 443 disclosure acknowledgment?
choice_a: Provide a copy of the signed acknowledgment to the buyer, seller, tenant, or landlord who signed it
choice_b: File the signed acknowledgment with the county clerk as part of the deed package
choice_c: Nothing further -- retaining an internal office copy fully satisfies the statute
choice_d: Submit the signed acknowledgment to DOS within 24 hours of signature
explanation: RPL Section 443 requires the agent to provide a copy of the signed acknowledgment to the consumer who signed it, not merely retain an internal record -- both obligations exist side by side.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(3) -- agent must furnish signed copy to consumer

question: A prospective seller refuses to sign the acknowledgment portion of the RPL Section 443 disclosure form. What must the agent do?
choice_a: Set forth, under oath or affirmation, a written declaration of the facts of the refusal
choice_b: Nothing -- a refusal to sign relieves the agent of any further disclosure-related obligation
choice_c: Immediately terminate the listing agreement, since a refusal automatically voids it
choice_d: Forge the seller's signature on the acknowledgment to complete the file
explanation: When a party refuses to sign the acknowledgment, RPL Section 443 requires the agent to set forth, under oath or affirmation, a written declaration of the facts of the refusal, preserving a documented record even without a signature.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(3) -- refusal-to-sign declaration requirement

question: How long must a licensee keep the written declaration documenting a consumer's refusal to sign the RPL Section 443 disclosure acknowledgment?
choice_a: Not less than three years -- the same minimum retention period that applies to signed acknowledgments
choice_b: There is no retention requirement for a refusal declaration, unlike a signed acknowledgment
choice_c: Only 90 days from the date of the refusal
choice_d: Permanently, for the life of the brokerage
explanation: The written declaration of a refusal to sign must be retained for not less than three years, mirroring the retention period the statute imposes on signed acknowledgments.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(3) -- three-year retention of refusal declaration

question: A buyer refuses to sign the RPL Section 443 disclosure acknowledgment, and the agent simply moves forward with the transaction without documenting anything about the refusal. What is the compliance problem?
choice_a: The agent failed to set forth a written declaration under oath or affirmation of the facts of the refusal, as RPL Section 443 requires when a party declines to sign
choice_b: There is no compliance problem, since a refusal to sign relieves the agent of any further obligation
choice_c: There is no compliance problem, since the disclosure requirement applies only to sellers, never to buyers
choice_d: The only problem is that the agent should have charged the buyer a penalty fee for refusing to sign
explanation: Simply proceeding without documentation after a refusal to sign leaves the agent out of compliance, since RPL Section 443 specifically requires a written, sworn declaration of the facts of the refusal in that situation.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(3) -- consequence of undocumented refusal

question: A brokerage's records-retention policy automatically purges all signed agency disclosure acknowledgments after two years. Does this comply with RPL Section 443?
choice_a: No -- the statute requires signed acknowledgments (and refusal declarations) to be retained for not less than three years, so a two-year purge falls short
choice_b: Yes -- two years exceeds any retention period the statute requires
choice_c: Yes -- RPL Section 443 does not address recordkeeping at all
choice_d: No, but only because two years is an unusually short period for any real estate record of any kind
explanation: Because RPL Section 443 sets a minimum three-year retention period for signed acknowledgments and refusal declarations, a policy that purges these records after only two years fails to meet the statutory minimum.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(3) -- minimum three-year recordkeeping requirement

question: RPL Section 443 contains an exemption in its subdivision addressing scope. Under that exemption, when does the section NOT apply to a real estate licensee's dealings with a buyer, seller, tenant, or landlord?
choice_a: When the licensee works with that party in accordance with terms the licensee and the party have agreed to, and in a capacity other than as an agent
choice_b: Whenever the transaction involves cash rather than mortgage financing
choice_c: Whenever the licensee has more than ten years of experience
choice_d: Whenever the party is represented by an attorney
explanation: RPL Section 443 does not apply when a licensee works with a buyer, seller, tenant, or landlord in a capacity other than as an agent, under terms the licensee and that party have agreed to -- a scope exemption distinct from the disclosure-timing and recordkeeping rules.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(5) -- non-agent capacity exemption

question: A licensed salesperson is personally selling a house they own, dealing directly with the buyer on their own behalf rather than representing a separate seller as agent. Does RPL Section 443's disclosure requirement apply to this sale?
choice_a: No -- because the licensee is dealing in a capacity other than as an agent (as a principal selling their own property), the statute's exemption applies
choice_b: Yes -- the statute applies to every transaction a licensee is involved in, regardless of capacity
choice_c: Yes, but only because the property is residential
choice_d: No, but only because the buyer happens to also be a licensee
explanation: Because RPL Section 443 exempts a licensee who deals with a party in a capacity other than as an agent, a licensee selling their own personally-owned property as a principal -- not representing another party -- falls outside the mandatory disclosure requirement.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(5) -- exemption applied to a licensee acting as principal

question: How does RPL Section 443 statutorily define an 'agent' for purposes of the section?
choice_a: A person licensed as a real estate broker, associate real estate broker, or real estate salesperson under RPL Section 440-a who is acting in a fiduciary capacity
choice_b: Any person, licensed or not, who assists in any part of a real estate transaction
choice_c: Only a broker who personally holds the listing agreement, never a cooperating salesperson
choice_d: Any attorney who represents a party in a real estate closing
explanation: RPL Section 443 defines 'agent' as a person licensed as a real estate broker, associate real estate broker, or real estate salesperson under Section 440-a who is acting in a fiduciary capacity -- both the licensure and fiduciary-capacity elements must be present.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(1) -- statutory definition of 'agent'

question: Under RPL Section 443's definitions, is a 'seller's agent' limited only to the original agent who took the listing?
choice_a: No -- the definition also includes an agent who cooperates with the listing agent, a seller's subagent, or a broker's agent who finds or obtains a buyer for the seller's property
choice_b: Yes -- only the specific individual who signed the original listing agreement can ever be a seller's agent
choice_c: No -- 'seller's agent' refers exclusively to the seller's attorney
choice_d: Yes -- cooperating agents from other firms can never qualify as seller's agents under any circumstance
explanation: RPL Section 443 defines 'seller's agent' broadly enough to cover a listing agent acting alone, a cooperating agent working with the listing agent, a seller's subagent, or a broker's agent who finds or obtains a buyer -- not just the original listing agent personally.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(1) -- 'seller's agent' definition

question: Under RPL Section 443's definitions, which of the following satisfies the definition of a 'buyer's agent'?
choice_a: Either an agent who contracts to locate residential real property for a buyer, or an agent who finds a buyer for a property and presents an offer to purchase to the seller or seller's agent while negotiating on the buyer's behalf
choice_b: Only an agent who has never had any prior contact with the seller or the seller's agent
choice_c: Only an agent who is also simultaneously the listing agent on the same property
choice_d: Only an agent who charges no commission to the buyer
explanation: RPL Section 443 defines 'buyer's agent' to cover either of two functions -- contracting to locate property for a buyer, or finding a buyer for a property and presenting an offer while negotiating on that buyer's behalf -- either one independently satisfies the definition.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(1) -- 'buyer's agent' definition

question: RPL Section 443 defines a 'dual agent' as an agent acting as a buyer's/tenant's agent and a seller's/landlord's agent under what specific condition?
choice_a: In the same transaction -- representing both sides of one particular deal, not merely representing different buyer and seller clients across separate, unrelated transactions
choice_b: At any point during the agent's career, regardless of whether the two roles occur in the same deal or in entirely separate deals
choice_c: Only when the agent personally holds an ownership interest in the brokerage
choice_d: Only when both parties are represented by the same brokerage but by two different, unaffiliated agents
explanation: The statutory definition of 'dual agent' requires that the buyer's/tenant's agent role and the seller's/landlord's agent role occur in the same transaction -- an agent who represents a buyer in one deal and separately represents a seller in an unrelated deal is not a dual agent under the statute.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(1) -- 'dual agent' requires same-transaction representation

question: An agent represented Buyer A in a transaction that closed last month. That same agent now represents Seller B in a completely unrelated new listing this month. Does this make the agent a 'dual agent' under RPL Section 443?
choice_a: No -- 'dual agent' status under the statute requires representing both a buyer/tenant and a seller/landlord in the same transaction, and these are two separate, unrelated transactions
choice_b: Yes -- representing a buyer in any past deal and a seller in any later deal always creates dual agency
choice_c: Yes -- once an agent has ever represented a buyer, every subsequent seller representation is automatically dual agency
choice_d: No, but only because more than 30 days separate the two transactions
explanation: Because RPL Section 443's dual agent definition is tied to representing both sides of the same transaction, representing a buyer in one closed deal and a seller in a wholly separate later deal does not create dual agency.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(1) -- 'dual agent' same-transaction requirement applied

question: How do a seller/landlord and buyer/tenant actually give their 'advance informed consent' to dual agency (or to dual agency with designated sales agents) under RPL Section 443?
choice_a: By indicating their consent choice directly on the agency disclosure form itself, which contains the consent language and checkbox options
choice_b: By verbally confirming consent to DOS over the phone
choice_c: By signing a separate court-filed affidavit unrelated to the disclosure form
choice_d: Advance informed consent cannot be given in writing under any circumstance -- only after-the-fact ratification is permitted
explanation: The advance informed consent to dual agency, or to dual agency with designated sales agents, is given by the parties indicating their choice directly on the disclosure form itself, which is built to capture that consent alongside the agency-relationship explanations.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(4); DOS Form 1736 -- consent captured on the disclosure form

question: Under RPL Section 443's definition of 'designated sales agent,' who is eligible to serve in that role?
choice_a: A licensed real estate salesperson or associate broker, working under the supervision of a real estate broker, who is assigned to represent one client when a different client is also represented by that same broker in the same transaction
choice_b: Only the broker of record personally, never a salesperson or associate broker
choice_c: Any unlicensed employee of the brokerage designated in writing by the broker
choice_d: Only an attorney retained separately by one of the parties
explanation: A 'designated sales agent' is defined as a licensed salesperson or associate broker who works under a supervising broker's oversight and is assigned to represent one client when the same broker also represents an opposing client in the same transaction -- a role distinct from the supervising broker.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(1) -- 'designated sales agent' definition

question: In a dual agency with designated sales agents arrangement, what is the status of the supervising real estate broker who makes the designations?
choice_a: The supervising broker is themselves considered a dual agent, even though each individually designated sales agent advocates for only one side of the transaction
choice_b: The supervising broker has no agency relationship with either party once the designations are made
choice_c: The supervising broker automatically becomes the designated agent for whichever side offers the higher commission
choice_d: The supervising broker is legally reclassified as a broker's agent once designations are made
explanation: Even though each designated sales agent individually represents and advocates for just one side, the real estate broker who represents both parties and makes the designations is itself considered a dual agent in that transaction.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(1),(4) -- supervising broker's status as dual agent

question: According to the New York agency disclosure form's own description of designated sales agency, how does a designated sales agent's duty to their assigned client compare to that of an exclusive single-party agent?
choice_a: A designated sales agent cannot provide the full range of fiduciary duties, including undivided loyalty, that an agent representing only one party in a non-dual-agency transaction can provide
choice_b: A designated sales agent provides identical, unmodified fiduciary duties to their client compared with an exclusive single-party agent, with no difference at all
choice_c: A designated sales agent owes greater fiduciary duties than an exclusive single-party agent, as compensation for the more complex office arrangement
choice_d: A designated sales agent owes fiduciary duties only to the supervising broker, not to the assigned client
explanation: Because the designated sales agent operates within a brokerage that also represents the other side through a different designated agent, the disclosure form itself acknowledges that a designated sales agent cannot provide the same full range of fiduciary duties -- including undivided loyalty -- that an exclusive single-party agent could provide.
source_note: DOS Form 1736 (Disclosure Regarding Real Estate Agency Relationships) -- designated agency's inherent limitation

question: Does RPL Section 443's agency disclosure requirement apply only to sales transactions, or also to residential leasing?
choice_a: It applies to both -- the statute's disclosure obligations run in parallel to landlord's agents and tenant's agents in residential leasing, just as they run to seller's agents and buyer's agents in sales
choice_b: It applies only to sales transactions; residential leasing/rental transactions are entirely outside the statute
choice_c: It applies only to leases longer than five years
choice_d: It applies to leasing only in New York City, not elsewhere in the state
explanation: RPL Section 443's definitions and disclosure triggers address landlords and tenants in parallel with sellers and buyers, so the agency disclosure requirement applies equally to residential leasing transactions and to sales transactions.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 443(1),(3) -- parallel treatment of sales and leasing transactions
